title: Reading the Prophets
summary: Who the prophets were and when they spoke, prophecy in the ancient Near East, the forms prophets used, how prophetic books were collected, prediction and fulfillment in the Old Testament and the New, and how to read an oracle in its own time before reading it in ours.

sections.body:
A prophet in the Bible is first of all a messenger: someone who has stood, as the Old Testament puts it, in the council of the LORD and comes out to speak his word to others. The most common Hebrew word is nabi, whose origin is debated; many scholars connect it to an Akkadian verb meaning to call, so that a prophet is either ‘one who is called’ or ‘one who calls out’. Older words were ro'eh and chozeh, both meaning ‘seer’, and 1 Samuel preserves a note that “the prophet of today was formerly called the seer” (1 Samuel 9:9). Prophets were also called ‘man of God’ and ‘servant of the LORD’.

The popular idea of a prophet is someone who predicts the future. Biblical prophets did speak of the future, but most of what they said was addressed to their own time: they confronted kings, condemned injustice and idolatry, called Israel back to the covenant, warned of judgment, and promised restoration beyond it. Scholars sometimes put it this way: the prophets were forthtellers more than foretellers, and when they foretold, it was to press a present decision. Amos says that God does nothing without revealing his plan to his servants the prophets, and that the prophet speaks because he cannot keep silent: “The Lord GOD has spoken— who will not prophesy?” (Amos 3:8).

Prophets came from every part of society. Isaiah moved in royal circles in Jerusalem. Jeremiah and Ezekiel were from priestly families. Amos insisted he was not a professional prophet, “nor was I the son of a prophet; rather, I was a herdsman and a tender of sycamore-fig trees” (Amos 7:14), where ‘son of a prophet’ refers to a member of the prophetic guilds of the time. Women prophesied too: Miriam (Exodus 15:20), Deborah (Judges 4:4), Huldah, who was consulted by King Josiah's officials when the Book of the Law was found in the temple (2 Kings 22:14-20), and in the New Testament Anna (Luke 2:36) and the four daughters of Philip (Acts 21:9).

The Old Testament knows two kinds of prophetic figures. Early prophets such as Samuel, Nathan, Gad, Ahijah, Elijah, Elisha, and Micaiah appear in the stories of Samuel and Kings but left no books of their own. From the eighth century BC onward come the prophets whose words were collected into books, sometimes called the writing or classical prophets. In the Jewish arrangement of the Hebrew Bible, the historical books Joshua, Judges, Samuel, and Kings are themselves called the Former Prophets, and Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and the Book of the Twelve (Hosea to Malachi, counted as one book because the twelve fit on a single scroll) are the Latter Prophets. Ben Sira, about 180 BC, already speaks of the twelve prophets as a group (Sirach 49:10). Christian Bibles call the first three the Major Prophets and the twelve the Minor Prophets, meaning shorter, not less important, and place Lamentations and Daniel among the prophets as well.

Every prophetic book belongs to a particular moment, and reading a prophet well begins with knowing which. Most prophetic books open with a heading that names the kings in whose reigns the prophet spoke (Isaiah 1:1; Hosea 1:1; Amos 1:1). The table below gives approximate dates for the writing prophets, grouped by the three great crises that called them out: the rise of Assyria in the eighth century, which ended the northern kingdom of Israel with the fall of Samaria in 722 BC; the rise of Babylon, which destroyed Jerusalem and its temple in 587 or 586 BC; and the return from exile after Cyrus of Persia conquered Babylon in 539 BC.

Some dates are secure because the books give them. Ezekiel dates many of his oracles to the day, counted from King Jehoiachin's exile in 597 BC, and Haggai and Zechariah date theirs to the reign of the Persian king Darius I. Others are uncertain. Joel and Obadiah name no king, and proposals range across several centuries. Jonah was a prophet in the reign of Jeroboam II (2 Kings 14:25), but when the book about him was written is debated, with dates proposed from the eighth century to after the exile. The authorship and date of parts of Isaiah and Zechariah are also debated, as a later section explains. The kings named here are set out in the guide to the kings of Israel and Judah.

sections.body:
Israel was not the only people with prophets. Letters found at Mari, an ancient city on the Euphrates excavated from 1933, include reports from the eighteenth century BC of men and women who delivered messages from gods to King Zimri-Lim, some in states of ecstasy, some warning him or urging a course of action. Seventh-century Assyrian archives preserve oracles given to the kings Esarhaddon and Ashurbanipal, many by prophets of the goddess Ishtar of Arbela, often with the reassurance ‘Do not fear’. An inscription discovered in 1967 at Deir Alla in Jordan, written on plaster in the eighth century BC, tells of a vision of ‘Balaam son of Beor’, the same seer who appears in Numbers 22 to 24, showing that his name was remembered east of the Jordan.

These texts show that the forms of biblical prophecy, the messenger speech, the vision report, the oracle of assurance, were known across the region. They also throw the distinctive features of Israel's prophets into relief. Most ancient Near Eastern prophecy served the king, supporting his rule and his wars. The biblical prophets were constantly in conflict with kings: Nathan confronts David, Elijah confronts Ahab, Jeremiah is imprisoned by Zedekiah's officials. Their words were addressed not only to rulers but to the whole people, and their chief concern was not military victory but covenant faithfulness, especially worship of the LORD alone and justice for the poor. And their words were collected, written down, and preserved as Scripture, even when, and often because, those words had condemned the very people who preserved them.

Abraham Heschel, in his study The Prophets (1962), argued that the heart of biblical prophecy is what he called the pathos of God: the prophets reveal a God who is personally affected by what his people do, who grieves and is angered and yearns, and the prophet shares that divine feeling. Walter Brueggemann's The Prophetic Imagination (1978) emphasized the prophets' task of criticizing the dominant order and energizing hope for an alternative. Both books, from a Jewish and a Christian scholar, have shaped how modern readers hear the prophets.

Prophetic books are mostly poetry, and they are made of shorter units, each with a recognizable form. Hermann Gunkel began the study of these forms, and Claus Westermann's Basic Forms of Prophetic Speech (German 1960, English 1967) set out the most influential account. Recognizing the form of a passage helps a reader see where it begins and ends and what it is doing.

The messenger formula, “This is what the LORD says”, is the signature of prophetic speech. In the ancient world a messenger repeated his master's words in the first person, and the prophets present themselves the same way: the ‘I’ of an oracle is often God's. The judgment speech, the most common form, pairs an accusation (the reason) with an announcement (the consequence), often linked by ‘therefore’. Amos's oracles against the nations open with the same frame for each: “For three transgressions of Damascus, even four, I will not revoke My judgment” (Amos 1:3), then name the crime and the punishment, until the pattern turns on Judah and Israel themselves in chapter 2.

The woe oracle begins with the cry hoy, used at funerals, as if the audience were already dead: “Woe to you who add house to house and join field to field until no place is left and you live alone in the land.” (Isaiah 5:8). The covenant lawsuit (in Hebrew rib) stages a courtroom, with heaven and earth or the mountains as witnesses: “Hear, O mountains, the LORD’s indictment” (Micah 6:2; compare Isaiah 1:2 and Hosea 4:1). The oracles against the nations (Amos 1 to 2; Isaiah 13 to 23; Jeremiah 46 to 51; Ezekiel 25 to 32) announce God's judgment on Israel's neighbors and oppressors and assert that he rules them all. The salvation oracle, often opening ‘Do not fear’, assures a frightened people of God's help (Isaiah 41:8-16).

Prophets also reported visions (Amos 7 to 8; Jeremiah 1:11-14; Ezekiel 1; Zechariah 1 to 6), often built on wordplay: Jeremiah sees an almond branch (shaqed) and God says he is watching (shoqed) over his word (Jeremiah 1:11-12). They told how God called them (Isaiah 6; Jeremiah 1; Ezekiel 1 to 3), in accounts that establish their authority. They performed symbolic acts: Isaiah walked naked and barefoot for three years as a sign of coming captivity (Isaiah 20:2-3), Jeremiah wore and then buried a linen belt and later carried a yoke (Jeremiah 13 and 27), Ezekiel lay on his side for months beside a model of besieged Jerusalem (Ezekiel 4), and Hosea's marriage to an unfaithful wife enacted God's relationship with Israel (Hosea 1 to 3). They lamented, as in Jeremiah's anguished complaints to God (the ‘confessions’ of Jeremiah 11 to 20), and argued, as Malachi does in a series of questions and answers.

A prophetic book is usually not a single speech or a diary in chronological order. It is a collection of oracles delivered over years, sometimes decades, gathered and arranged by the prophet, his disciples, or later scribes. Isaiah speaks of binding up his testimony among his disciples (Isaiah 8:16). Jeremiah dictated his oracles to the scribe Baruch, and when King Jehoiakim cut up and burned the scroll column by column, Jeremiah dictated it again with additions (Jeremiah 36). The books are often arranged by theme or form rather than by date: Jeremiah's dated passages jump back and forth across the reigns of the last kings of Judah.

The texts of some books survive in more than one form. The Greek translation of Jeremiah is about one-seventh shorter than the Hebrew and places the oracles against the nations in the middle of the book rather than at the end. Hebrew fragments of Jeremiah found at Qumran include copies of both the shorter and the longer form, which shows that both circulated in Hebrew before the time of Christ. The book introduction to Jeremiah in this Study Bible discusses what that means.

The most debated case is Isaiah. Jewish and Christian tradition received all sixty-six chapters as the work of Isaiah son of Amoz, who prophesied in the late eighth century. From the late eighteenth century, scholars such as J. C. Döderlein and J. G. Eichhorn argued that chapters 40 to 66 address the exiles in Babylon two centuries later and name Cyrus of Persia (Isaiah 44:28 and 45:1), and so come from a later prophet or prophets; Bernhard Duhm in 1892 further separated chapters 56 to 66. Most critical scholars now speak of First, Second, and Third Isaiah, while many also stress, following Brevard Childs and others, that the book was shaped to be read as a whole. Conservative scholars such as E. J. Young, J. Alec Motyer, and John Oswalt have defended the unity of the book, arguing that predictive prophecy is exactly what the book claims for itself (Isaiah 41:21-29 and 46:9-10 make the ability to announce the future the proof of the LORD's deity), that the vocabulary and themes are consistent throughout, and that the New Testament cites passages from both halves under Isaiah's name. The complete Isaiah scroll from Qumran (1QIsaa, copied in the second century BC) presents the whole book as one scroll. Readers should know that the debate exists and that it turns in part on convictions about whether God reveals the future.

When prophets did speak of the future, their words work in several different ways, and treating them all alike causes confusion.

Many prophecies are conditional, even when they do not say so. God explains the principle in Jeremiah 18: if he announces disaster on a nation and it turns from its evil, “then I will relent of the disaster I had planned to bring” (Jeremiah 18:8), and the reverse. Jonah proclaims, “Forty more days and Nineveh will be overturned!” (Jonah 3:4), with no condition attached; Nineveh repents, and God relents (3:10), much to Jonah's displeasure. A century after Micah predicted that Jerusalem would become a heap of rubble, the elders of Judah recalled that his prophecy had not come to pass in his day because King Hezekiah feared the LORD and the LORD relented (Jeremiah 26:18-19). Prophecies of judgment were meant to produce repentance, and they succeeded when they were not fulfilled.

Deuteronomy gives a test for false prophets: “When a prophet speaks in the name of the LORD and the message does not come to pass or come true, that is a message the LORD has not spoken.” (Deuteronomy 18:22). It also warns that a prophet whose sign does come true but who leads the people to other gods is to be rejected (Deuteronomy 13:1-5). Jeremiah's confrontation with Hananiah, who promised that the exile would end in two years (Jeremiah 28), shows the test at work: the prophet who promised peace had to wait for events to vindicate him.

Other prophecies look far beyond the prophet's own time: the promise of a new covenant written on the heart (Jeremiah 31:31-34), a king from David's line who will reign in justice (Isaiah 9:6-7; 11:1-10), a ruler from Bethlehem (Micah 5:2), the outpouring of the Spirit on all flesh (Joel 2:28-32), a servant who suffers for others (Isaiah 52:13 to 53:12). The prophets often saw these future events together, as a traveler sees distant mountain ranges in one view without the valleys between them, so that return from exile, the coming king, and the renewal of all creation appear side by side. Peter says the prophets themselves searched to understand “the time and setting to which the Spirit of Christ in them was pointing” (1 Peter 1:11).

sections.h: How the New Testament reads the prophets
sections.body:
The New Testament writers read the prophets as pointing to Jesus. Jesus himself, according to Luke, explained to two disciples “what was written in all the Scriptures about Himself”, beginning with Moses and all the Prophets (Luke 24:27). But the New Testament uses the prophets in more than one way, and seeing how helps the reader.

Some texts are read as direct prediction: Micah 5:2, on the ruler from Bethlehem, is cited in Matthew 2:6 as the answer the scribes gave Herod. Others are read typologically, where a pattern in Israel's history is repeated and completed in Jesus. Matthew 2:15 quotes Hosea 11:1, “Out of Egypt I called My Son”, which in Hosea looks back to the exodus and speaks of Israel as God's son. Matthew is not claiming Hosea predicted a child's return from Egypt; he is saying that Jesus relives and fulfills Israel's story, the true Son who does what Israel failed to do. The Greek word for fulfill, plēroō, means to fill full, and can be used of a pattern brought to completion as well as of a prediction coming true.

Isaiah 7:14 is the best-known test case. In its setting, about 734 BC, the prophet offers King Ahaz a sign during a war against Syria and Israel: a young woman (Hebrew ‘almah, a young woman of marriageable age) will bear a son named Immanuel, and before the child is old enough to know good from evil, the two threatening kings will be gone (7:16). The Septuagint translated ‘almah with parthenos, usually ‘virgin’, and Matthew quotes that Greek text of Jesus' birth (Matthew 1:23). Readers have understood the relation in several ways. Some, such as E. J. Young and J. Alec Motyer, read the verse as a direct prophecy of the virgin birth, with the sign to Ahaz tied to the timescale of that future child's life. Many others see a double reference: a child born in Ahaz's day fulfilled the sign then, and Matthew sees its fuller meaning in Jesus, the true ‘God with us’. Jewish interpreters, such as Rashi in the eleventh century, identified the young woman as Isaiah's wife or Ahaz's wife and the child as a son born in that generation, and read Matthew's use as a misreading. Critical scholars generally read the verse as addressed only to Ahaz's time. The Christian confession of the virgin birth rests on the Gospels' own accounts in Matthew and Luke; the question here is how Matthew is reading Isaiah.

The Servant Songs of Isaiah (42:1-9; 49:1-13; 50:4-11; 52:13 to 53:12) raise a similar question. When the Ethiopian official asks Philip whether the prophet speaks of himself or someone else (Acts 8:34), Philip tells him about Jesus. Jewish interpreters, from Rashi onward, have commonly identified the servant with Israel, which Isaiah itself calls ‘my servant’ (Isaiah 41:8; 49:3), while earlier Jewish readings, such as the Targum, applied parts of chapter 53 to the Messiah. Christians read the servant as Israel's true representative, the one who does for Israel and the nations what Israel could not, and see the song fulfilled in the death and resurrection of Jesus. Raymond Brown's 1955 study of the sensus plenior, the ‘fuller sense’ that God intended in a text beyond what its human author fully grasped, gave a name to one way of holding the original meaning and the New Testament meaning together.

sections.h: Reading an oracle in its own time
sections.body:
The single most useful habit in reading the prophets is to read an oracle first as its first hearers heard it. Find the setting: which king, which crisis, which audience. The book's heading and the historical notes in this Study Bible will help. Find the boundaries of the unit, since chapter divisions are later additions and a single chapter may hold several oracles; look for the messenger formula, a change of addressee, or a new form. Identify the form: accusation and announcement, woe, lawsuit, vision, promise. Read the poetry as poetry, with its parallel lines and its images, and do not press the images into literal predictions they were never meant to be.

Then ask what the oracle meant for the people who first heard it, and only after that ask how it speaks to the church and the world now. Jeremiah 29:11, “For I know the plans I have for you, declares the LORD, plans to prosper you and not to harm you, to give you a future and a hope”, is often quoted as a personal promise of success. In context it is a letter to the exiles in Babylon, telling them to settle down, build houses, and “Seek the prosperity of the city to which I have sent you as exiles” (29:7), because the exile will last seventy years, most of them beyond their own lifetimes. The promise is real, and Christians rightly take comfort in it, but its comfort is deeper and harder than a promise of good fortune: God has plans for his people even in the long defeat.

The prophets' central themes carry across time without much translation. They insist that worship without justice is hateful to God: “I hate, I despise your feasts!” (Amos 5:21), and instead “let justice roll on like a river, and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream” (5:24). They insist on loyalty to God alone and expose every substitute, whether a foreign god, a military alliance, or the temple itself treated as a guarantee (“Do not trust in deceptive words”, Jeremiah 7:4). They announce judgment as the consequence of covenant unfaithfulness, and they refuse to let judgment be the last word, promising a restoration that only God can bring. Jesus drew on this tradition directly when he twice quoted Hosea: “I desire mercy, not sacrifice” (Matthew 9:13; 12:7, from Hosea 6:6).

Hebrews opens by saying that God “spoke to our fathers through the prophets” in many ways, and has now spoken by his Son (Hebrews 1:1-2). The New Testament also knows prophets in the church (Acts 11:27-28; 1 Corinthians 14), and Christians differ on whether and how that gift continues today, a second-order question on which faithful churches disagree. But they agree that the prophets of Israel remain Scripture, God's word spoken first to a particular people in a particular hour, and through them to every generation.
